title: Linear equations
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Name the unknown, write what the words say, then do the same to both sides. Stuck? Open a hint.

mistakes.why: Undo adding $[[b]]$ by SUBTRACTING $[[b]]$ from both sides.

hints: First take $[[b]]$ away from both sides.
$[[a]]x = [[c-b]]$. Now divide both sides by $[[a]]$.
problems.solution: Take $[[b]]$ from both sides: $[[a]]x = [[c-b]]$. Divide by $[[a]]$: $x = [[n]]$. Check: $[[a]] \times [[n]] + [[b]] = [[c]]$ ✓.

mistakes.why: Move $[[c]]x$ by SUBTRACTING it from both sides: that leaves $[[a-c]]x$, not $[[a+c]]x$.

hints: Get the $x$ terms on one side: subtract $[[c]]x$ from both sides.
$[[a-c]]x - [[b]] = [[d]]$. Now add $[[b]]$ to both sides.

problems.prompt: Solve $\frac{x}{[[p]]} + \frac{x}{[[q]]} = [[s]]$.

mistakes.why: $\frac{x}{[[p]]} + \frac{x}{[[q]]}$ is not $\frac{x}{[[p+q]]}$. Multiply both sides by $[[lcm(p,q)]]$ to clear the fractions.

hints: Multiply both sides by $[[lcm(p,q)]]$, which both $[[p]]$ and $[[q]]$ go into.
That gives $[[lcm(p,q)/p]]x + [[lcm(p,q)/q]]x = [[s*lcm(p,q)]]$.
problems.solution: Multiply by $[[lcm(p,q)]]$: $[[lcm(p,q)/p]]x + [[lcm(p,q)/q]]x = [[s*lcm(p,q)]]$, so $[[lcm(p,q)/p + lcm(p,q)/q]]x = [[s*lcm(p,q)]]$ and $x = [[v]]$. Check: $\frac{[[v]]}{[[p]]} + \frac{[[v]]}{[[q]]} = [[v/p]] + [[v/q]] = [[s]]$ ✓.

problems.prompt: The sum of four consecutive even numbers is $[[4*n+12]]$. What is the smallest of them?

mistakes.why: That is the largest. The question asks for the smallest.
That is their average, which falls between two of the even numbers. Write them as $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$, $n + 6$.

hints: Call them $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$ and $n + 6$.
Their sum is $4n + 12 = [[4*n+12]]$.

problems.prompt: Five less than three times a number is the same as the number increased by $[[k]]$. What is the number?

mistakes.why: "Five less than three times a number" means take $5$ away: $3x - 5$, not $3x + 5$.

hints: "Five less than three times a number" is $3x - 5$.
Solve $3x - 5 = x + [[k]]$.

title: Linear equations challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: If $4(x - 3) = 2x + 6$, what is $x$?

why.B: $4(x - 3)$ is $4x - 12$, not $4x - 3$: multiply both terms in the bracket.

problems.prompt: The sum of five consecutive whole numbers is $105$. What is the product of the smallest and the largest?

why.D: $441 = 21^2$ is the middle number squared. The smallest and largest are $19$ and $23$.

problems.solution: The middle number is the average: $\frac{105}{5} = 21$. The numbers are $19$ to $23$, and $19 \times 23 = 437$, choice (B). (Shortcut: $(21 - 2)(21 + 2) = 441 - 4$.)

problems.prompt: When $7$ is added to two-thirds of a number, the result is $5$ more than half of the number. What is the number?

why.D: Check the sign: $\frac{2}{3}x - \frac{1}{2}x = 5 - 7 = -2$, so $\frac{x}{6}$ is negative.

problems.prompt: A pen costs $3$ dollars more than a pencil. Four pens and six pencils cost $27$ dollars in all. How many dollars does one pencil cost?

why.E: That is the price of a pen. The question asks for a pencil.

problems.solution: Let a pencil cost $p$. Then $4(p + 3) + 6p = 27$, so $10p + 12 = 27$ and $p = 1.5$ dollars, choice (B). Check: pens cost $4.5$, and $18 + 9 = 27$ ✓.

problems.prompt: For which value of $a$ does the equation $a(x - 2) = 6x + 4$ have NO solution?

why.A: With $a = -2$ the equation becomes $-8x = 0$, which has the solution $x = 0$.

problems.solution: Rearrange: $ax - 2a = 6x + 4$, so $(a - 6)x = 2a + 4$. If $a = 6$, this says $0 = 16$: no $x$ works. For any other $a$ we can divide by $a - 6$ and get one solution. So $a = 6$, choice (E).

title: Systems of equations
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Add or subtract the equations to cancel a letter, and look for a shortcut to what is asked. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: Two numbers add up to $[[x+y]]$ and differ by $[[x-y]]$. What is the larger number?

mistakes.why: That is the smaller number.
That is halfway between them. The larger one is half the difference, $[[(x-y)/2]]$, above that.

hints: Write $a + b = [[x+y]]$ and $a - b = [[x-y]]$.
Add the two equations: $2a = [[2*x]]$.
problems.solution: Adding $a + b = [[x+y]]$ and $a - b = [[x-y]]$ gives $2a = [[2*x]]$, so the larger number is $[[x]]$ (and the smaller is $[[y]]$).

problems.prompt: If $[[a]]x + [[b]]y = [[a*p+b*q]]$ and $[[a]]x - [[b]]y = [[a*p-b*q]]$, what is $x$?

mistakes.why: That is $y$. The question asks for $x$.

hints: Add the two equations: the $y$ terms cancel.
problems.solution: Adding the equations cancels $y$: $[[2*a]]x = [[2*a*p]]$, so $x = [[p]]$. (Subtracting them gives $[[2*b]]y = [[2*b*q]]$, so $y = [[q]]$.)

problems.prompt: If $[[m]]x + [[n]]y = [[m*p+n*q]]$ and $[[n]]x + [[m]]y = [[n*p+m*q]]$, what is $x + y$?

mistakes.why: That is $[[m+n]](x + y)$. Divide by $[[m+n]]$.

hints: You don't need $x$ and $y$ on their own. Add the two equations.
Adding gives $[[m+n]]x + [[m+n]]y = [[(m+n)*(p+q)]]$.
problems.solution: Add the equations: $[[m+n]]x + [[m+n]]y = [[(m+n)*(p+q)]]$, so $[[m+n]](x + y) = [[(m+n)*(p+q)]]$ and $x + y = [[p+q]]$.

problems.prompt: A show sold $[[t]]$ tickets for $[[8*a + 5*(t-a)]]$ dollars in all. Adult tickets cost $8$ dollars and child tickets $5$ dollars. How many adult tickets were sold?

mistakes.why: That is the number of child tickets.

hints: Let $a$ be the adult tickets, so $[[t]] - a$ are child tickets.

problems.prompt: The lines $y = [[m]]x - [[b]]$ and $y = [[c]] - [[k]]x$ cross at one point. What is the $x$-coordinate of that point?

mistakes.why: That is the $y$-coordinate. The question asks for $x$.

hints: Where the lines cross, both $y$ values are equal: $[[m]]x - [[b]] = [[c]] - [[k]]x$.
problems.solution: Set the $y$ values equal: $[[m]]x - [[b]] = [[c]] - [[k]]x$, so $[[m+k]]x = [[b+c]]$ and $x = [[n]]$. (Then $y = [[m]] \times [[n]] - [[b]] = [[m*n-b]]$.)

title: Systems challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set.

problems.prompt: If $x + y = 12$ and $x - y = 4$, what is $xy$?
problems.solution: Adding gives $2x = 16$, so $x = 8$ and $y = 4$. Then $xy = 32$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: If $5a + 2b = 31$ and $2a + 5b = 25$, what is $a + b$?
problems.solution: Add the equations: $7a + 7b = 56$, so $a + b = 8$, choice (C). You never need $a$ and $b$ on their own.

problems.prompt: A farm has only chickens and cows. Together they have $50$ heads and $140$ legs. How many cows are there?

why.D: That is the number of chickens.

problems.solution: If all $50$ were chickens there would be $100$ legs. Each cow adds $2$ more legs, and there are $40$ extra, so there are $20$ cows, choice (B). (As a system: $h + w = 50$ and $2h + 4w = 140$.)

problems.prompt: If $x + y = 10$, $y + z = 14$ and $x + z = 16$, what is $x + y + z$?

why.E: $40$ counts every letter twice: it is $2(x + y + z)$.

problems.solution: Add all three: each letter appears twice, so $2(x + y + z) = 40$ and $x + y + z = 20$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: For which value of $k$ do the equations $2x + 3y = 7$ and $kx + 6y = 9$ have NO common solution?

why.A: With $k = 2$ the lines have different slopes, so they cross once.

problems.solution: Doubling the first equation gives $4x + 6y = 14$. If $k = 4$, the second says $4x + 6y = 9$: the same left side can't equal both $14$ and $9$, so there is no solution (the lines are parallel). For any other $k$ the lines cross. So $k = 4$, choice (C).

title: Distance, rate and time
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Use $d = rt$, keep the units matched, and decide whether speeds add or subtract. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: Two cyclists start $[[(u+v)*t]]$ km apart and ride towards each other at $[[u]]$ km/h and $[[v]]$ km/h. After how many hours do they meet?

mistakes.why: They ride TOWARDS each other, so the gap closes at the sum of the speeds, $[[u]] + [[v]]$.

hints: How much does the gap shrink each hour?
The gap shrinks by $[[u]] + [[v]] = [[u+v]]$ km each hour.
problems.solution: The gap closes at $[[u]] + [[v]] = [[u+v]]$ km/h, so they meet after $\frac{[[(u+v)*t]]}{[[u+v]]} = [[t]]$ hours.

problems.prompt: A car drives $[[d]]$ km in $[[m]]$ minutes. What is its average speed, in km/h?

mistakes.why: That is km per MINUTE. An hour has $60$ minutes.

hints: $[[m]]$ minutes is $\frac{[[m]]}{60}$ of an hour.
Speed $= \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = [[d]] \div \frac{[[m]]}{60}$.
problems.solution: $[[m]]$ minutes is $\frac{[[m]]}{60}$ hours, so the speed is $[[d]] \div \frac{[[m]]}{60} = \frac{[[d]] \times 60}{[[m]]} = [[60*d/m]]$ km/h.

problems.prompt: A dog chases a cat that is $[[w*t]]$ m ahead. The dog runs at $[[v+w]]$ m/s and the cat at $[[v]]$ m/s, in the same direction. After how many seconds does the dog catch the cat?

mistakes.why: They run the SAME way, so the gap closes at the difference of the speeds, not the sum.

hints: Each second, how much closer does the dog get?
The gap closes by $[[v+w]] - [[v]] = [[w]]$ m each second.
problems.solution: The gap closes at $[[v+w]] - [[v]] = [[w]]$ m/s, so the dog catches the cat after $\frac{[[w*t]]}{[[w]]} = [[t]]$ seconds.

problems.prompt: Ben cycles to school. At $10$ km/h he arrives $[[p]]$ minutes late; at $15$ km/h he arrives $[[q]]$ minutes early. How far is school, in km?
hints: The two trips take $[[p]] + [[q]] = [[p+q]]$ minutes apart. Write that in hours.
problems.solution: The times differ by $[[p+q]]$ minutes, or $\frac{[[p+q]]}{60}$ hours. So $\frac{d}{10} - \frac{d}{15} = \frac{d}{30} = \frac{[[p+q]]}{60}$, and $d = \frac{[[p+q]]}{2} = [[(p+q)/2]]$ km.

problems.prompt: Mia jogs up a trail at $[[u]]$ km/h and back down the same trail at $[[v]]$ km/h. The round trip takes $[[t]]$ hours. How long is the trail, in km?

mistakes.why: That uses the average of the two speeds. She spends longer at the slower speed: write each part's time as distance $\div$ speed.

hints: Call the length $d$. Going up takes $\frac{d}{[[u]]}$ hours and coming down $\frac{d}{[[v]]}$ hours.

title: Distance, rate and time challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set.

problems.prompt: A train travels $240$ km at $80$ km/h, then $150$ km at $100$ km/h. How many hours does the whole trip take?
problems.solution: The first part takes $\frac{240}{80} = 3$ hours and the second $\frac{150}{100} = 1.5$ hours: $4.5$ hours in all, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Two cars are $378$ km apart and drive towards each other, one at $60$ km/h and the other at $66$ km/h. After how many hours do they meet?

why.E: That is how long the first car alone would take. Both cars close the gap.

problems.solution: The gap closes at $60 + 66 = 126$ km/h, so they meet after $\frac{378}{126} = 3$ hours, choice (B).

problems.prompt: Tom leaves home walking at $5$ km/h. One hour later his sister follows him on a bike at $15$ km/h. How many minutes after she leaves does she catch up with him?

why.B: That uses her full speed. The gap closes at $15 - 5 = 10$ km/h, because Tom keeps walking.

problems.solution: When she leaves, Tom is $5$ km ahead. The gap closes at $15 - 5 = 10$ km/h, so she catches him after $\frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}$ hour: $30$ minutes, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Walking up a moving escalator, Lia reaches the top in $20$ seconds. Standing still on it, she takes $30$ seconds. How many seconds would she take to walk up it if it were switched off?

why.A: Times don't subtract. Her walking SPEED is the difference of the two speeds.

problems.solution: Say the escalator is $60$ steps long. Walking on it she covers $3$ steps a second; the escalator alone moves $2$ steps a second. So her own walking speed is $1$ step a second, and $60$ steps take $60$ seconds, choice (D).

problems.prompt: A boat goes $24$ km downstream in $2$ hours and comes back upstream in $3$ hours. What is the speed of the current, in km/h?

why.C: $4$ is the difference between the two speeds. The current adds on the way down and subtracts on the way up, so it is HALF that difference.
why.E: $10$ is the boat's speed in still water.

problems.solution: Downstream: $\frac{24}{2} = 12$ km/h $=$ boat $+$ current. Upstream: $\frac{24}{3} = 8$ km/h $=$ boat $-$ current. Subtracting, $2 \times$ current $= 4$, so the current is $2$ km/h, choice (B).

title: Work and mixtures
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. For work, add the rates. For mixtures, follow the pure part. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: Pat can mow a lawn in $[[a]]$ hours and Sam can mow it in $[[b]]$ hours. Working together, how many hours does it take them?

mistakes.why: That averages the times. Working together they are faster than either one alone.
Adding the times means one works after the other. Add their RATES: $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]}$.

hints: Pat mows $\frac{1}{[[a]]}$ of the lawn per hour and Sam $\frac{1}{[[b]]}$.
Together they mow $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a + 1/b]]$ of the lawn per hour.
problems.solution: Together they mow $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a + 1/b]]$ of the lawn per hour, so the lawn takes $1 \div [[1/a + 1/b]] = [[a*b/(a+b)]]$ hours.

problems.prompt: A tap fills a tub in $[[a]]$ minutes, and the drain empties a full tub in $[[b]]$ minutes. With the tap on and the drain open, how many minutes does it take to fill the tub?

mistakes.why: The drain works AGAINST the tap: subtract its rate instead of adding it.

hints: The tap adds $\frac{1}{[[a]]}$ of the tub per minute; the drain takes away $\frac{1}{[[b]]}$.
Each minute the tub gains $\frac{1}{[[a]]} - \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a - 1/b]]$.
problems.solution: Each minute the tub gains $\frac{1}{[[a]]} - \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a - 1/b]]$ of its volume, so it fills in $1 \div [[1/a - 1/b]] = [[a*b/(b-a)]]$ minutes.

problems.prompt: How many litres of pure water must be added to $[[v]]$ litres of $[[p]]\%$ salt water to make it $[[q]]\%$ salt?

mistakes.why: That is the total volume at the end. Take away the $[[v]]$ litres you started with.

hints: Adding water doesn't change the amount of salt: $\frac{[[p]]}{100} \times [[v]] = [[v*p/100]]$ litres.
At the end that salt is $[[q]]\%$ of the total, so the total is $[[v*p/100]] \div \frac{[[q]]}{100}$.
problems.solution: The salt stays the same: $[[v*p/100]]$ litres. For it to be $[[q]]\%$, the total must be $\frac{[[v*p/100]]}{[[q/100]]} = [[v*p/q]]$ litres. So add $[[v*p/q]] - [[v]] = [[v*(p-q)/q]]$ litres of water.

problems.prompt: $[[a]]$ litres of $[[p]]\%$ juice are mixed with $[[b]]$ litres of $[[q]]\%$ juice. What percent juice is the mix? Type just the number.

mistakes.why: That averages the percents, as if there were equal amounts of each. Follow the litres of juice.

hints: Juice: $\frac{[[p]]}{100} \times [[a]] + \frac{[[q]]}{100} \times [[b]]$ litres.
That is $[[(a*p+b*q)/100]]$ litres of juice out of $[[a+b]]$ litres.
problems.solution: Juice: $[[a*p/100]] + [[b*q/100]] = [[(a*p+b*q)/100]]$ litres out of $[[a+b]]$ litres. As a percent: $\frac{[[(a*p+b*q)/100]]}{[[a+b]]} \times 100 = [[(a*p+b*q)/(a+b)]]\%$.

problems.prompt: $[[w]]$ workers build a wall in $[[d]]$ days. At the same rate, how many days would $[[v]]$ workers take?

mistakes.why: More workers means FEWER days. The days go the other way: find the worker-days first.

hints: The wall takes $[[w]] \times [[d]] = [[w*d]]$ worker-days of work.
Share those $[[w*d]]$ worker-days among $[[v]]$ workers.
problems.solution: The wall is $[[w]] \times [[d]] = [[w*d]]$ worker-days of work. With $[[v]]$ workers it takes $\frac{[[w*d]]}{[[v]]} = [[w*d/v]]$ days.

title: Work and mixtures challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set.

problems.prompt: Ivy can paint a room in $4$ hours and Max can paint it in $12$ hours. Working together, how many hours do they take?

why.D: That averages the times. Together they are faster than Ivy alone.
why.E: That adds the times, as if one painted after the other.

problems.solution: Together they paint $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the room per hour, so they take $3$ hours, choice (A).

problems.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can each fill a pool on their own in $6$, $10$ and $15$ hours. With all three open, how many hours does it take?
problems.solution: Together: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{5 + 3 + 2}{30} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the pool per hour, so it takes $3$ hours, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many litres of $60\%$ acid must be mixed with $10$ litres of $20\%$ acid to make a $30\%$ acid mix?

why.E: Equal amounts would give the average, $40\%$, not $30\%$.
why.B: Check: $10$ litres of $20\%$ and $3$ of $60\%$ hold $3.8$ litres of acid out of $13$: about $29\%$.

problems.prompt: Lea can do a job alone in $10$ days and Rob can do it alone in $15$ days. Lea works alone for $4$ days, then Rob joins her. How many more days do they need to finish the job?

why.E: $6$ days is how long the WHOLE job takes them together. Lea has already done part of it.

problems.solution: In $4$ days Lea does $\frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$ of the job, leaving $\frac{3}{5}$. Together they do $\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{6}$ per day, so they need $\frac{3}{5} \div \frac{1}{6} = \frac{18}{5} = 3.6$ days, choice (B).

problems.prompt: A $40$ kg alloy is $25\%$ copper. How many kg of pure copper must be added to make it $40\%$ copper?

why.A: $6$ kg is $15\%$ of $40$, but adding copper also makes the total heavier. Check: $16$ out of $46$ kg is only about $35\%$.

problems.solution: There are $0.25 \times 40 = 10$ kg of copper. Adding $x$ kg: $10 + x = 0.4(40 + x) = 16 + 0.4x$, so $0.6x = 6$ and $x = 10$ kg, choice (C). Check: $20$ out of $50$ kg is $40\%$ ✓.

title: Ages, coins and money
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Make a table: for ages, one column per time; for coins, one equation for how many and one for how much. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: Leo is $[[a]]$ years old and his mother is $[[m]]$. In how many years will his mother be exactly twice as old as Leo?

mistakes.why: That is their age difference, which never changes. Write both ages in $x$ years.

hints: In $x$ years Leo is $[[a]] + x$ and his mother is $[[m]] + x$.
problems.solution: In $x$ years: $[[m]] + x = 2([[a]] + x) = [[2*a]] + 2x$, so $x = [[m]] - [[2*a]] = [[m-2*a]]$. Check: Leo will be $[[a + m - 2*a]]$ and his mother $[[m + m - 2*a]]$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Kim is $[[k]]$ years older than Jay. $[[y]]$ years ago, Kim was three times as old as Jay. How old is Jay now?

mistakes.why: That is how old Jay was $[[y]]$ years ago. Add the $[[y]]$ years back.

hints: $[[y]]$ years ago, call Jay's age $j$. Kim was then $j + [[k]]$.
$j + [[k]] = 3j$, because the age difference never changes.
problems.solution: $[[y]]$ years ago Jay was $j$ and Kim $j + [[k]] = 3j$, so $j = [[k/2]]$. Now Jay is $[[k/2]] + [[y]] = [[k/2+y]]$.

problems.prompt: Jo has $[[n]]$ coins, all nickels ($5$ cents) and dimes ($10$ cents). They are worth $[[5*n+5*d]]$ cents in all. How many dimes are there?

mistakes.why: That is the number of nickels.

hints: If all $[[n]]$ were nickels they would be worth $[[5*n]]$ cents.
Each dime adds $5$ cents more than a nickel.
problems.solution: All nickels would be worth $[[5*n]]$ cents. The extra $[[5*n+5*d]] - [[5*n]] = [[5*d]]$ cents come from dimes, $5$ cents extra each: $[[d]]$ dimes. (As a system: $5([[n]] - d) + 10d = [[5*n+5*d]]$.)

problems.prompt: A father is $[[k*(s-x)+x]]$ years old and his son is $[[s]]$. How many years ago was the father exactly $[[k]]$ times as old as his son?
hints: Call it $t$ years ago. Then the father was $[[k*(s-x)+x]] - t$ and the son $[[s]] - t$.
problems.solution: $t$ years ago: $[[k*(s-x)+x]] - t = [[k]]([[s]] - t) = [[k*s]] - [[k]]t$. So $[[k-1]]t = [[k*s]] - [[k*(s-x)+x]] = [[(k-1)*x]]$ and $t = [[x]]$. Check: the father was $[[k*(s-x)]]$ and the son $[[s-x]]$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Sara buys $[[n]]$ stamps, some at $[[p]]$ cents and the rest at $[[q]]$ cents. She pays $[[p*a + q*(n-a)]]$ cents in all. How many $[[p]]$-cent stamps did she buy?

mistakes.why: That is how many $[[q]]$-cent stamps she bought.

hints: Let $a$ be the $[[p]]$-cent stamps, so $[[n]] - a$ are $[[q]]$-cent stamps.

title: Ages, coins and money challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set.

problems.prompt: Ella is $12$ and her aunt is $40$. In how many years will her aunt be exactly twice as old as Ella?

why.E: $28$ is their age difference, which never changes.
why.C: $14$ would make the aunt $54$ and Ella $26$: not quite twice.

problems.solution: In $x$ years: $40 + x = 2(12 + x) = 24 + 2x$, so $x = 16$, choice (D). Check: $56 = 2 \times 28$ ✓.

problems.prompt: A jar has $30$ coins, all dimes ($10$ cents) and quarters ($25$ cents), worth $510$ cents in all. How many quarters are there?

why.D: That is the number of dimes.

problems.solution: All dimes would be worth $300$ cents. Each quarter adds $15$ cents more, and there are $210$ extra cents, so there are $\frac{210}{15} = 14$ quarters, choice (C). Check: $16 \times 10 + 14 \times 25 = 160 + 350 = 510$ ✓.

problems.prompt: A mother's and her daughter's ages add up to $50$. Five years ago the mother was $4$ times as old as the daughter. How old is the daughter now?

why.B: Five years ago their ages added up to $40$, not $50$: both were $5$ years younger.

problems.solution: Let the daughter be $d$, so the mother is $50 - d$. Five years ago: $45 - d = 4(d - 5) = 4d - 20$, so $5d = 65$ and $d = 13$, choice (D). Check: $8$ and $32$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Movie tickets cost $7$ dollars for students and $11$ dollars for adults. A group of $12$ paid $112$ dollars. How many adults were in the group?

why.B: That is the number of students.

problems.solution: All students would cost $84$ dollars. Each adult costs $4$ more, and there are $28$ extra dollars, so there are $7$ adults, choice (D). Check: $5 \times 7 + 7 \times 11 = 35 + 77 = 112$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Max has only nickels, dimes and quarters. He has $3$ times as many dimes as quarters, and $2$ more nickels than dimes. His coins are worth $290$ cents. How many coins does he have?

why.A: Count all three kinds: $4$ quarters, $12$ dimes AND $14$ nickels.

problems.solution: Let $q$ be the quarters: $3q$ dimes and $3q + 2$ nickels. Value: $25q + 30q + 5(3q + 2) = 70q + 10 = 290$, so $q = 4$. That is $4 + 12 + 14 = 30$ coins, choice (C).

title: Warm-up for the check
instructions: Five quick problems, one from each lesson. Type each answer and press Check. Hints are here, but not in the check.

mistakes.why: Undo the bracket: divide by $[[a]]$, then ADD $[[b]]$.

hints: Divide both sides by $[[a]]$ first.

problems.prompt: If $x + y = [[x+y]]$ and $x - y = [[x-y]]$, what is $y$?

mistakes.why: That is $x$. Subtract the equations to find $y$.

hints: Subtract the second equation from the first: the $x$'s cancel.

problems.prompt: A runner covers $[[d]]$ km in $[[m]]$ minutes. What is her average speed, in km/h?

mistakes.why: That is km per minute. Multiply by $60$ for km per hour.

hints: $[[m]]$ minutes is $\frac{[[m]]}{60}$ of an hour.

problems.prompt: Pipe A fills a tank in $[[a]]$ hours and pipe B fills it in $[[b]]$ hours. With both open, how many hours does it take?

mistakes.why: That averages the times. Add the rates instead.

hints: Together they fill $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]}$ of the tank per hour.
problems.solution: $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a + 1/b]]$ of the tank per hour, so it takes $[[a*b/(a+b)]]$ hours.

problems.prompt: Ravi is $[[r]]$ and his sister is $[[s]]$. In how many years will Ravi be exactly twice as old as his sister?

mistakes.why: That is their age difference, which never changes.

title: ⭐ Unit 3 check
instructions: Eight AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first, no hints. You need all 8 right to pass. Each try gives you different problems.

why.D: Moving $-[[b]]$ to the other side makes it $+[[b]]$.
why.E: Subtract $[[c]]x$ from both sides: that leaves $[[a-c]]x$, not $[[a+c]]x$.

problems.solution: Subtract $[[c]]x$ and add $[[b]]$: $[[a-c]]x = [[b+d]]$, so $x = [[n]]$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: The sum of four consecutive odd numbers is $[[4*n+12]]$. What is the largest of them?

why.B: That is their average, which isn't even odd. Write them as $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$, $n + 6$.

problems.solution: Write them as $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$, $n + 6$: $4n + 12 = [[4*n+12]]$, so $n = [[n]]$ and the largest is $[[n+6]]$, choice (D).

problems.prompt: If $\frac{x + 2}{3} - \frac{x - 1}{4} = 2$, what is $x$?
For which value of $a$ does the equation $3(ax - 2) = 12x + 5$ have NO solution?

why.E: The $x$ terms must match: $3a = 12$, so $a = 4$, not $12$.

problems.solution: $3ax - 6 = 12x + 5$, so $(3a - 12)x = 11$. If $3a = 12$, this says $0 = 11$: no solution. So $a = 4$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Two numbers add up to $[[x+y]]$ and differ by $[[x-y]]$. What is the smaller number?

why.C: That is halfway between the two numbers.
why.D: That is the difference, not a number.

problems.solution: Subtracting the equations $a + b = [[x+y]]$ and $a - b = [[x-y]]$ gives $2b = [[2*y]]$, so the smaller number is $[[y]]$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: If $[[m]]x + [[n]]y = [[m*p+n*q]]$ and $[[n]]x + [[m]]y = [[n*p+m*q]]$, what is $x + y$?

why.E: Adding the equations gives $[[m+n]](x + y)$. Divide by $[[m+n]]$.

problems.solution: Add the equations: $[[m+n]]x + [[m+n]]y = [[(m+n)*(p+q)]]$, so $x + y = [[p+q]]$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A farm has only chickens and pigs. Together they have $35$ heads and $94$ legs. How many pigs are there?

why.D: That is the number of chickens.
why.E: $24$ is the number of extra legs. Each pig has $2$ more legs than a chicken.

problems.solution: If all $35$ were chickens there would be $70$ legs. The $24$ extra legs come from pigs, $2$ extra each: $12$ pigs, choice (B).

problems.prompt: If $a + b = 13$, $b + c = 17$ and $a + c = 20$, what is $c$?

why.E: $25$ is $a + b + c$. Now take away $a + b$.

problems.solution: Adding all three: $2(a + b + c) = 50$, so $a + b + c = 25$ and $c = 25 - 13 = 12$, choice (D).

problems.prompt: Two trains start $[[(u+v)*t]]$ km apart and travel towards each other at $[[u]]$ km/h and $[[v]]$ km/h. After how many hours do they meet?

why.B: They move TOWARDS each other, so the gap closes at the sum of the speeds.
why.C: That is how long the first train alone would take to cover the whole gap.

problems.solution: The gap closes at $[[u]] + [[v]] = [[u+v]]$ km/h, so they meet after $\frac{[[(u+v)*t]]}{[[u+v]]} = [[t]]$ hours, choice (A).

problems.prompt: A car leaves town at $[[v]]$ km/h. $[[h]]$ hours later a second car leaves the same town on the same road at $[[u]]$ km/h. How many hours after it leaves does the second car catch up?

why.B: The cars go the same way, so the gap closes at the DIFFERENCE of the speeds.
why.C: That counts from when the FIRST car left.

problems.solution: When the second car leaves, the first is $[[v]] \times [[h]] = [[v*h]]$ km ahead. The gap closes at $[[u]] - [[v]] = [[u-v]]$ km/h, so it takes $\frac{[[v*h]]}{[[u-v]]} = [[v*h/(u-v)]]$ hours, choice (A).

problems.prompt: Driving at $60$ km/h, Rae arrives $10$ minutes late. Driving at $80$ km/h, she arrives $5$ minutes early. How far does she drive, in km?
problems.solution: The times differ by $15$ minutes $= \frac{1}{4}$ hour: $\frac{d}{60} - \frac{d}{80} = \frac{d}{240} = \frac{1}{4}$, so $d = 60$ km, choice (C). Check: $1$ hour versus $45$ minutes ✓.

problems.prompt: A boat travels $36$ km downstream in $2$ hours and returns upstream in $3$ hours. What is the boat's speed in still water, in km/h?

why.A: $3$ km/h is the speed of the current.
why.E: $18$ km/h is the downstream speed, with the current's help.

problems.solution: Downstream: $18$ km/h $=$ boat $+$ current. Upstream: $12$ km/h $=$ boat $-$ current. Adding, $2 \times$ boat $= 30$, so the boat goes $15$ km/h in still water, choice (D).

problems.prompt: Ana can do a job in $[[a]]$ hours and Bea can do it in $[[b]]$ hours. Working together, how many hours do they take?

why.B: That averages the times. Together they are faster than either one alone.
why.C: That adds the times, as if one worked after the other.
why.E: That is how long Ana takes alone.

problems.solution: Together: $\frac{1}{[[a]]} + \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a + 1/b]]$ of the job per hour, so they take $[[a*b/(a+b)]]$ hours, choice (A).

problems.prompt: A tap fills a sink in $[[a]]$ minutes. The drain empties a full sink in $[[b]]$ minutes. With both open, how many minutes does it take to fill the sink?

why.A: That adds the two rates. The drain works AGAINST the tap: subtract its rate.
why.B: Times don't subtract. Subtract the RATES: $\frac{1}{[[a]]} - \frac{1}{[[b]]}$.

problems.solution: Each minute the sink gains $\frac{1}{[[a]]} - \frac{1}{[[b]]} = [[1/a - 1/b]]$ of its volume, so it fills in $[[a*b/(b-a)]]$ minutes, choice (C).

problems.prompt: $[[a]]$ litres of $[[p]]\%$ juice are mixed with $[[b]]$ litres of $[[q]]\%$ juice. What percent of the mix is juice?

why.B: That averages the percents, as if there were equal amounts of each.
why.C: That swaps the amounts: there are $[[a]]$ litres of the $[[p]]\%$ juice.

problems.solution: Juice: $[[a*p/100]] + [[b*q/100]] = [[(a*p+b*q)/100]]$ litres out of $[[a+b]]$, which is $[[(a*p+b*q)/(a+b)]]\%$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: How many grams of pure gold must be added to $60$ grams of a $50\%$ gold alloy to make a $70\%$ gold alloy?

why.B: Check: $20$ g makes $50$ g of gold out of $80$ g, only $62.5\%$. The added gold also makes the total heavier.

problems.solution: There are $30$ g of gold. Adding $x$ g: $30 + x = 0.7(60 + x) = 42 + 0.7x$, so $0.3x = 12$ and $x = 40$ g, choice (D). Check: $70$ out of $100$ g ✓.

problems.prompt: A mother is $[[m]]$ years old and her son is $[[s]]$. In how many years will she be exactly twice his age?

why.B: That is their age difference, which never changes.

problems.prompt: A purse has $[[n]]$ coins, all nickels ($5$ cents) and quarters ($25$ cents), worth $[[5*(n-q)+25*q]]$ cents in all. How many quarters are there?

why.A: That is the number of nickels.

problems.solution: All nickels would be worth $[[5*n]]$ cents. Each quarter adds $20$ cents more, and there are $[[20*q]]$ extra cents, so there are $[[q]]$ quarters, choice (B).

problems.prompt: Three years ago, Nia was twice as old as Omar. In five years, their ages will add up to $49$. How old is Nia now?
problems.solution: Now Nia is $N$ and Omar $O$. Three years ago: $N - 3 = 2(O - 3)$, so $N = 2O - 3$. In five years: $N + O + 10 = 49$, so $N + O = 39$. Then $3O - 3 = 39$, $O = 14$ and $N = 25$, choice (D).
